name: Kowalski-Glikman's Eleven Dimensional Wave
description: An eleven dimensional supergravity wave with parallel null 4-form flux and 32 Killing spinors. Three transverse directions focus at twice the frequency of the other six.
convention: We use mostly plus signature, with $c$ explicit in the line element and the exterior form. The component basis uses $cu$. The Ricci contraction is $R_{MN}=R^P{}_{MPN}$, where $M,N,P,Q,R,S$ label the eleven spacetime coordinates.
history: Neighbouring light rays refocus at two different rates in the gravitational wave Jerzy Kowalski-Glikman found in 1984 [kowalski1984, figueroa2001, marolf2002]. His solution belongs to eleven dimensional supergravity, whose bosonic fields are the spacetime metric and a 4-form field strength [figueroa2001]. A parallel null flux supports the wave, and nine spatial directions lie across its propagation [figueroa2001].¶Christopher Hull constructed exact pp-waves of eleven dimensional supergravity in the same year, allowing both an antisymmetric tensor field and a Rarita-Schwinger field [hull1984]. Some of these solutions admit Killing spinors, the spinor fields that describe preserved supersymmetries [hull1984, figueroa2001]. For Kowalski-Glikman's wave the fermionic fields vanish, and the coupled metric and flux admit 32 independent Killing spinors, preserving all the supersymmetry of the theory [figueroa2001].¶José Figueroa-O'Farrill and George Papadopoulos returned to the solution in 2001 and calculated its symmetry superalgebra [figueroa2001]. They placed it in a family of Lorentzian symmetric plane waves with parallel 4-form flux [figueroa2001]. Spatial rotations preserve separate groups of three and six transverse directions, and the continuous spacetime symmetry group has dimension 38 [figueroa2001].¶The two groups of directions have different tidal accelerations [figueroa2001]. Along geodesics parametrised by the null coordinate $cu$, the three directions threaded by the flux oscillate at frequency $\mu/3$, and the other six at $\mu/6$, where $\mu$ measures the flux [figueroa2001, marolf2002]. The scalar curvature vanishes, while the Riemann tensor produces this repeated focusing [figueroa2001]. At a caustic, neighbouring rays meet and the Rosen coordinates fail; the spacetime remains smooth and geodesically complete [blau2002penrose].¶Matthias Blau, Figueroa-O'Farrill, Hull, and Papadopoulos obtained the wave as a Penrose limit in 2002 [blau2002penrose]. Following a light ray with motion on the sphere and magnifying its neighbourhood takes either $\mathrm{AdS}_4\times S^7$ or $\mathrm{AdS}_7\times S^4$ to the same eleven dimensional wave [blau2002penrose]. The ratio of the curvature radii of the two factors fixes the ratio of its transverse frequencies [blau2002penrose].¶Figueroa-O'Farrill and Papadopoulos published a local classification of the maximally supersymmetric solutions in 2003 [figueroa2003maximally]. In eleven dimensional supergravity, Minkowski space, the two anti-de Sitter products with spheres, and Kowalski-Glikman's wave exhaust the possibilities up to local isometry [figueroa2003maximally]. Every nonzero value of $\mu$ describes the same wave geometry after a rescaling of the two null coordinates [figueroa2001, figueroa2003maximally].

related.text: The symmetric plane wave family with an arbitrary constant transverse matrix. Kowalski-Glikman's solution fixes this matrix through its null flux and maximal supersymmetry [figueroa2001].
Anti-de Sitter space of four dimensions times a 7-sphere. Its Penrose limit along a light ray with motion on the sphere is Kowalski-Glikman's wave [blau2002penrose].
The maximally supersymmetric wave of type IIB supergravity, in ten dimensions with a null 5-form. Its eight transverse directions share one frequency [figueroa2003maximally].
The parallel null rays of a pp-wave extend to eleven dimensions, with nine transverse directions and a parallel 4-form supporting the homogeneous tidal curvature [figueroa2001].

coordinates.name: Brinkmann

parameters.description: The positive flux scale, an inverse length. In the Brinkmann chart $F=\mu c\,du\wedge dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3$, with $F_{u123}=\mu$ in the component basis $cu$. The field equation is $R_{MN}=\frac1{12}(F_{MPQR}F_N{}^{PQR}-\frac1{12}g_{MN}F_{PQRS}F^{PQRS})$ [figueroa2001].

coordinates.convention: The coordinates $u$ and $v$ are null, with $u$ a time and $v$ a length; $x_1$ to $x_9$ are transverse lengths. Components use $x^0=cu$. A dot denotes differentiation with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot u=d(cu)/d\lambda$. The global chart has $F=\mu c\,du\wedge dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3$ [figueroa2001].

coordinates.name: Rosen

parameters.description: The positive flux scale, an inverse length. In the Brinkmann chart $F=\mu c\,du\wedge dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge dx_3$, with $F_{u123}=\mu$ in the component basis $cu$. The field equation is $R_{MN}=\frac1{12}(F_{MPQR}F_N{}^{PQR}-\frac1{12}g_{MN}F_{PQRS}F^{PQRS})$ [figueroa2001].

coordinates.convention: The Rosen patch has $0<u<3\pi/(\mu c)$, with $w$ and $y_1$ to $y_9$ lengths. Put $a_i=\sin(\omega_i cu)$, where $\omega_i=\mu/3$ for $i=1,2,3$ and $\omega_i=\mu/6$ for $i=4,\ldots,9$. The Brinkmann map is $x_i=a_i y_i$, $v=w+\frac12\sum_{i=1}^9a_i a_i\prime y_i^2$, where $a_i\prime=da_i/d(cu)$. The flux is $F=\mu c\,a_1a_2a_3\,du\wedge dy_1\wedge dy_2\wedge dy_3$. Components use $cu$; dots are affine derivatives. The patch ends at coordinate caustics [blau2002penrose].
